prize_parts.citation: for developing formal theory, and testing it empirically, on how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic performance

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B027 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. The exchange changed two things. I have narrowed the citation to the framework and its testable implications, so it does not imply that every constitutional or electoral-rule effect is causally settled. I have also decided that the Persson-Tabellini pair is an acceptable fallback, not a rival configuration. The case is that this work turned political institutions into an object of formal economic analysis. It explains why electoral systems, constitutions and fiscal capacity produce systematically different policies across states, and it ties those explanations to comparative and historical evidence. It has been absorbed into public economics, macroeconomics and comparative politics. The core is about three decades old, so it has been replicated, extended and criticised, and maturity is not an issue. On the chair's question about the third name, the trio's citation would lose the state-capacity, accountability and political-selection strand without Besley. That strand is not part of the constitutions-and-electoral-rules programme and it supports the fiscal-capacity half of the citation. Under one stated weighting of conceptual originality, maturity, identification quality and attribution tractability, with equal weights, I order B027 first, B002 second and B015 third. B002 beats B027 on identification, B015 and B027 are both mature, and B027 and B002 are the more tractable on attribution. The ordering is sensitive. If identification quality counted roughly double, B002 would lead, and if maturity counted double, B015 would gain. I give this as a weighting, separate from the fallback preferences above. Opening support counts are not evidence of merit, and the explicit preferences in round 1 (three each for B002 and B027) show no convergence that I should try to manufacture. I considered a two-part configuration. Under the three-unique-person cap, no second part can be added to a three-name B027 without dropping a laureate, so I propose one part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains identification. Much of the evidence on electoral rules and constitutions comes from cross-country comparisons in which institutional adoption is endogenous. I build cross-national datasets in my own work, so I know where that evidence is thin. The contribution is more secure as a framework with sharp predictions than as a set of causally settled coefficients, and the design-based evidence in B002 is easier to evaluate directly. Second, the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity is adjacent, and the committee may reasonably regard this as a timing question even if the science differs. I presented that prize, so I may overstate the contrast. Third, Besley's claim is strong but complementary to the Persson-Tabellini core, and others on the committee reasonably regard the pair as the cleanest attribution. Fourth, political economics has many prominent contributors outside the three names, so any trio is contestable, though less so than in B015.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B002 first and B027 only as an alternative. She says the identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than in design-based work, that my own concession on this point matters under common criteria, and that B027 needs separating from the 2024 prize and its theory-versus-evidence credit is hard to divide.
responses.response: I concede the identification point and have written it into the citation. The citation now credits the formal framework and its empirical testing, not the causal settlement of each institutional effect. I do not think identification alone should decide the ordering, because the framework produced the predictions that later, more design-based work on local rules and accountability could test. That is an argument about durability, not about the cross-country coefficients, and you may reasonably weigh it less. On the 2024 boundary, the distinction I drew in round 1 stands, namely institutions taken as given and their effect on policy choices versus the origins of institutions and long-run prosperity. If you and others still find the proximity too close, I would treat it as a question of timing, not as a scientific objection to the programme. I also accept that if the committee places a premium on directly checkable evidence, B002 is the stronger candidate on that criterion, and I list it first among my alternatives.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B004 first and B027 third. He says B027 has among the cleanest attribution structures on the shortlist, but notes the 2024 proximity and the weaker cross-country identification. He argues that B004 gets more weight for the breadth of its macro-financial mechanism and policy use, and that its 2008 test supports maturity.
responses.response: I take the attribution agreement seriously. I want to apply the evidence standard to both candidates equally. You accept that the aggregate evidence for the collateral mechanism is indirect or calibrated, and the 2008 crisis is confirmation of relevance, not identification. B027's cross-country evidence has the same limitation in a different form. I therefore do not think identification quality separates B004 from B027, and the difference turns on the overlap questions. For B004 that is the 2022 prize and Gertler's credit, and for B027 it is the 2024 prize. Your own and Andersson's willingness to fall back to a Kiyotaki-Moore pair suggests B004's attribution is as tractable as mine. I do not think breadth of policy use alone favours it, since fiscal and electoral institutions are also a policy question. I would not call either candidate decisively stronger on science.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first. He argues that population-scale administrative data made mobility measurable and place-specific, that the mobility atlas results have been checked and extended, and that the citation should stay close to what is best confirmed. He keeps Katz off the three-name cap.
responses.response: I agree with the way the citation is framed. A citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs is the defensible version of B002, and with that wording I do not think the maturity concern is decisive on merit. My ordering of B027 above B002 rests on two things that your reply does not remove. The first is that most of the core results are under a decade old and the causal reading of place effects is still debated, so the same test of time has not been run. The second is that, even with the strongest argument for Chetty, Hendren and Friedman, the Katz question is a judgement call under the cap that leaves one credited name out, whereas B027 faces a smaller third-name question. As someone who builds measurement infrastructure myself, I value the data contribution as a scientific advance, not as a lesser kind of result. If the committee concludes that replication in other administrative datasets is already enough, I would see B002 as a legitimate first choice and not a compromise.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B027 first and moved in round 1 from the Persson-Tabellini pair to the trio with Besley, arguing that the state-capacity and political-selection strand is not derivative. He weighs identification more heavily than a theorist would and sees the 2024 prize as a timing consideration only.
responses.response: I agree with the reasons for the trio, and also with treating the 2024 prize as a timing consideration, not a scientific one. I should not count your move as independent corroboration of my own view, since the argument is the same one I made and we are both on record for B027. For the committee's purposes the argument for Besley should be judged on whether state capacity and political selection are separable from the constitutions-and-electoral-rules strand. I think they are, and I have said what the citation would lose without them. Your weighting of identification is what keeps this from being an easy first choice for either of us. I also share your view that timing is a legitimate committee consideration, but it argues about which year, not whether the science qualifies.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the 2024 institutions prize as bearing on novelty or only on timing, and whether the distinction between taking institutions as given and explaining their origins is accepted as substantive.

How much the weaker cross-country identification should count against B027 relative to the design-based evidence in B002, and how far the later quasi-experimental work on local rules and accountability carries the empirical case.
Whether Besley is the right third name or whether the Persson-Tabellini pair is the cleaner attribution, and how contributors outside the credited names should be treated.

Whether B002's long-run causal claims will be settled enough to change the comparison, and whether a citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs would be sufficient for those who raise maturity.
My ordering depends on the weighting stated above and moves with it. I draw on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files and have not independently verified citations or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No credited name for B027, B002 or B015 is a listed collaborator or institutional connection in my profile. Disclosures, none of them adjudicated: (1) My field, comparative political institutions, measurement of democracy and state-building, is close to B027, and my political-science background could make me more receptive to the field. (2) I gave the 2024 presentation speech on the institutions prize, which bears on my contrast between that prize and B027. The speech may reflect collective drafting and does not establish a private preference. (3) My profile lists a co-author named Persson (with Rothstein, on corruption as a collective-action problem) without a first name. I have no basis in the profile for treating this as the credited Torsten Persson, so I flag the coincidence of surnames and do not assert a connection. (4) A colleague's file refers to Persson's past committee service as a disclosed conflict, and my profile does not establish anything about it. (5) I was at Lund from 2006 to 2021 and Enflo's file notes Lund colleagues on the committee, including Andersson. Enflo also prefers B027, so our agreement should not be read as independent corroboration. (6) I am at Stockholm University in a different department from committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, who prefer B015 or B002.
